## Introduction

In Lab 7, k-means put every thyroid patient in exactly one cluster. At the end
we said that a patient on the border between two groups needs a different
tool. This lab uses that tool, the **Gaussian mixture model (GMM)**, on a
classic clinical question:

> *Can glucose and insulin tests, with no diagnosis given, separate normal
> patients from patients with early and with full diabetes? And can the method
> tell us which patients are hard to place?*

We know the diagnosis for these patients, so we can check the answer. In real
unsupervised work there is no answer key. The lab shows what to look at then.

The plan:

1. **Look at the data.** Three tests, and clusters that are long and thin.
2. **k-means first.** Where it goes wrong, and why.
3. **EM by hand.** We write the E-step and the M-step from the slides, and
   watch the fit improve.
4. **Read the fitted model.** Weights, means, and covariances in clinical
   units.
5. **Soft assignment.** The probability that each patient belongs to each
   cluster, and who is uncertain.
6. **Choosing $K$.** BIC against the silhouette.
7. **Choosing the covariance shape.** Full, diagonal, or spherical.
8. **Starting points.** EM can stop at a bad answer.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR, so you do not need to
install R. Packages and data load once when the page opens. Give it a few
seconds on first load. Click **Run Code** to run a cell. Run the cells in
order from the top, because later cells use objects that earlier cells make.

## A note on the tools

Two choices in this lab differ from earlier labs.

- **`caret` does the preprocessing.** As in Lab 7, clustering has no outcome,
  so `train()` does not apply. We use `preProcess()` to center and scale.
- **We write EM ourselves.** The `mclust` package fits GMMs in one line, but
  it is not available in the browser. So we code the algorithm from the
  slides, using `dmvnorm()` from the `mvtnorm` package for the normal density.
  It is about 30 lines. We checked the code against `mclust` on these data:
  the log-likelihood and BIC agree.

## The data: glucose tolerance in 145 adults

Reaven and Miller (1979) studied 145 non-obese adults. Each person had
three measurements:

| Column | Test | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `glucose` | glucose response | area under the plasma glucose curve during a 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test |
| `insulin` | insulin response | area under the plasma insulin curve during the same test |
| `sspg` | steady-state plasma glucose | how well the body responds to insulin. A **high** value means **insulin resistance** |

Doctors also gave each person a diagnosis: **Normal**, **Chemical** diabetes
(an abnormal glucose test but no symptoms yet), or **Overt** diabetes (clinical
diabetes). We hide the diagnosis from the algorithm and use it only to check.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

dia <- read.csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("Normal", "Chemical", "Overt")))

tests <- dia |> select(-class)   # the three tests: all the algorithm sees

dim(dia)
table(dia$class)
```

### What a clinician expects

The median of each test, by diagnosis:

```{webr}
dia |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), median), n = n())
```

Overt patients have the highest glucose and insulin responses, by a wide
margin. Chemical patients have a glucose response close to normal, but their
`sspg` is the highest. Their cells respond poorly to insulin. This is the
early stage of the disease. Normal patients are low on all three tests.

### The shape of the groups

```{webr}
library(gridExtra)

p1 <- ggplot(dia, aes(glucose, insulin, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) + ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "glucose vs insulin") + theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p2 <- ggplot(dia, aes(insulin, sspg, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) + ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "insulin vs sspg") + theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1)
round(sapply(tests, sd), 1)
```

Three things are visible:

- **The scales differ.** The SD of `insulin` is 320. The SD of `glucose` is 64.
  We scale before clustering, as in Lab 7.
- **The groups are not round.** The overt patients lie along a long, thin
  band. The normal patients form a small blob with a thin tail. The groups
  have different sizes and different orientations.
- **The chemical and normal groups overlap** in `glucose`, and the chemical
  and overt groups overlap in `insulin`.

A clinician would say: some patients are borderline. We will check whether the
algorithm finds them.

```{webr}
library(caret)

pp <- preProcess(tests, method = c("center", "scale"))
z  <- as.matrix(predict(pp, tests))     # scaled tests: n = 145, p = 3
n  <- nrow(z)
p  <- ncol(z)
```

# Part 1 — k-means first

Lab 7 gave us k-means, so we start there. We use $K = 3$ and many starts.
To compare cluster numbers with diagnoses, we give the clusters a fixed
order: from the lowest to the highest mean `glucose`. This puts "Normal,
Chemical, Overt" in the same order as the diagnoses.

```{webr}
# number clusters 1, 2, 3 by increasing mean glucose, so labels are comparable
relabel <- function(cl) {
  ord <- order(tapply(tests$glucose, cl, mean))
  match(cl, ord)
}

set.seed(42)
km <- kmeans(z, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
km_cl <- relabel(km$cluster)

table(diagnosis = dia$class, cluster = km_cl)
mean(km_cl == as.integer(dia$class))   # share of patients in the "right" cluster
```

About three patients in four are in the "right" cluster. The mistakes are
large. Only 13 of the 36 chemical patients land in their own cluster, and 23
go into the normal cluster. Also, 9 of the 33 overt patients end up in the
normal cluster. Here is the picture:

```{webr}
dia |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km_cl)) |>
  ggplot(aes(glucose, insulin, colour = cluster, shape = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "k-means clusters (colour) vs. diagnosis (shape)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Why does k-means fail?** k-means assigns each patient to the nearest
centroid by Euclidean distance. The boundary between two clusters is a
straight line halfway between their centroids. So k-means implicitly assumes
that every cluster is a round ball of the same size. These clusters are long
and thin, and they have different sizes. A long thin cluster is cut in two,
or it takes patients from its neighbours.

A GMM fixes this by giving each cluster its **own** mean, its **own**
covariance matrix (size, shape, and orientation), and its **own** weight.

# Part 2 — EM by hand

The slides define the model: each cluster $k$ has a weight $\pi_k$, a mean
$\mu_k$, and a covariance $\Sigma_k$. The density of a patient is
$$p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, N(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k).$$
We do not know the cluster of any patient, so we use EM. It alternates two
steps.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Do this on paper first

In class we derived the E-step and the M-step for **two** clusters. Before you
read the code, write them out for **three** clusters ($K = 3$):

1. Write the model: the three weights $\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3$ (what must they
   add up to?), the three means, and the three covariances.
2. Write the E-step for $r_{n1}$, $r_{n2}$ and $r_{n3}$. How many terms are in
   the denominator now? What must $r_{n1} + r_{n2} + r_{n3}$ equal?
3. Write the M-step for $N_k$, $\hat\mu_k$, $\hat\Sigma_k$ and $\hat\pi_k$.
   Check that $N_1 + N_2 + N_3 = N$.
4. Which lines changed from the two-cluster case? (Only the number of terms
   changes. The formulas keep the same form for any $K$.)

Then compare your answer with the formulas and the code below.
:::

**E-step.** Given the parameters, compute for each patient $n$ and cluster $k$
the probability that the patient belongs to the cluster (the
**responsibility**):
$$r_{nk} = \hat P(Y = k \mid x_n) =
\frac{\pi_k \, N(x_n \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j \, N(x_n \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}.$$

**M-step.** Given the responsibilities, update the parameters. Each patient
counts in cluster $k$ with weight $r_{nk}$:
$$N_k = \sum_n r_{nk}, \quad
\hat\mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_n r_{nk}\, x_n, \quad
\hat\Sigma_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_n r_{nk}\,(x_n - \hat\mu_k)(x_n - \hat\mu_k)^\top, \quad
\hat\pi_k = \frac{N_k}{N}.$$

The formulas hold for any $K$, and the code follows them line by line. The
comments in the code show what happens when $K = 3$.

```{webr}
library(mvtnorm)

# E-step: responsibilities r[n, k], and the log-likelihood of the data
e_step <- function(z, pi_k, mu, Sigma) {
  K <- length(pi_k)                         # K = 3: pi_k has 3 numbers
  # numerator of r[n, k] for every k: pi_k * N(x_n | mu_k, Sigma_k)
  # K = 3: one column per cluster, so dens has 3 columns
  dens <- sapply(1:K, function(k) pi_k[k] * dmvnorm(z, mu[k, ], Sigma[[k]]))
  dens <- matrix(dens, nrow(z), K)
  # denominator = sum over k of the numerators; K = 3: a sum of 3 terms
  list(r = dens / rowSums(dens),            # normalize each row to sum to 1
       loglik = sum(log(rowSums(dens))))
}

# M-step: weighted means, covariances and weights
# (cov_type is used in Part 6; "full" is the usual GMM)
m_step <- function(z, r, cov_type = "full") {
  K  <- ncol(r)                             # K = 3: r has 3 columns
  Nk <- colSums(r)                          # N_k; K = 3: N_1 + N_2 + N_3 = N
  # mu_k = (1 / N_k) * sum_n r[n, k] * x_n, one row per cluster
  mu <- t(sapply(1:K, function(k) colSums(r[, k] * z) / Nk[k]))
  Sigma <- lapply(1:K, function(k) {        # K = 3: a list of 3 matrices
    d <- sweep(z, 2, mu[k, ])               # x_n - mu_k for every patient
    S <- crossprod(d * r[, k], d) / Nk[k]
    if (cov_type == "diag")      S <- diag(diag(S))
    if (cov_type == "spherical") S <- diag(mean(diag(S)), ncol(z))
    S + diag(1e-6, ncol(z))                 # tiny ridge keeps S invertible
  })
  list(pi_k = Nk / nrow(z), mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)   # pi_k = N_k / N
}
```

Now the loop. EM needs a starting point. We start from the k-means clusters:
we treat them as hard responsibilities (0 or 1), run one M-step to get
starting parameters, and then alternate E and M until the log-likelihood stops
changing. At the end we number the clusters by increasing `glucose`, as before.

```{webr}
fit_gmm <- function(z, K, cov_type = "full", init = NULL,
                    max_iter = 500, tol = 1e-8) {
  if (is.null(init))
    init <- if (K == 1) rep(1, nrow(z)) else kmeans(z, K, nstart = 10)$cluster
  r   <- diag(K)[init, , drop = FALSE]      # hard 0/1 responsibilities
  par <- m_step(z, r, cov_type)
  ll  <- numeric(0)
  for (i in 1:max_iter) {
    e  <- e_step(z, par$pi_k, par$mu, par$Sigma)
    ll <- c(ll, e$loglik)
    if (i > 1 && abs(ll[i] - ll[i - 1]) < tol) break   # converged
    if (i == max_iter) break
    par <- m_step(z, e$r, cov_type)
  }
  o <- order(par$mu[, 1])                   # number clusters by mean glucose
  list(pi_k = par$pi_k[o], mu = par$mu[o, , drop = FALSE],
       Sigma = par$Sigma[o], r = e$r[, o, drop = FALSE],
       loglik = ll, cov_type = cov_type)
}

set.seed(42)
gmm3 <- fit_gmm(z, K = 3)

length(gmm3$loglik)     # number of EM iterations
tail(gmm3$loglik, 1)    # final log-likelihood
```

EM stopped after a few dozen iterations. The log-likelihood is the quantity
EM increases at every step, never decreases:

```{webr}
ggplot(data.frame(iter = seq_along(gmm3$loglik), loglik = gmm3$loglik),
       aes(iter, loglik)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "EM iteration", y = "log-likelihood",
       title = "EM never decreases the log-likelihood") +
  theme_bw()

all(diff(gmm3$loglik) >= -1e-8)
```

It rises fast at first, then slowly. EM is guaranteed to climb, but it
climbs to a **local** maximum. Part 7 returns to this.

### Watching the clusters move

We stop EM after 1, 3, 10 and 45 iterations, and draw each cluster as an
ellipse (the 95% region of its normal distribution). Iteration 1 is the
k-means start, with its hard assignments.

```{webr}
# points on the 95% ellipse of N(mu, Sigma), mapped back to clinical units
ellipse_df <- function(mu, Sigma, level = 0.95, npts = 100) {
  th  <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = npts)
  e   <- eigen(Sigma)
  pts <- sqrt(qchisq(level, df = 2)) *
    cbind(cos(th), sin(th)) %*% diag(sqrt(e$values)) %*% t(e$vectors)
  pts <- sweep(pts, 2, mu, "+")
  data.frame(x = pts[, 1] * pp$std[1] + pp$mean[1],
             y = pts[, 2] * pp$std[2] + pp$mean[2])
}

ellipses_of <- function(f, cols = c(1, 2)) {
  bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(f$pi_k), function(k) {
    ellipse_df(f$mu[k, cols], f$Sigma[[k]][cols, cols]) |>
      mutate(cluster = factor(k))
  }))
}

snap <- function(t) {
  set.seed(42)
  f <- fit_gmm(z, K = 3, max_iter = t)
  ellipses_of(f) |> mutate(step = paste("iteration", t))
}

ell <- bind_rows(snap(1), snap(3), snap(10), snap(45)) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = paste("iteration", c(1, 3, 10, 45))))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dia, aes(glucose, insulin), colour = "grey50", size = 1.5) +
  geom_path(data = ell, aes(x, y, colour = cluster), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ step, nrow = 1) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(x = "glucose", y = "insulin") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Iteration 1 is the fit to the k-means labels. Over the next iterations, the
big ellipse (overt) widens to cover the whole band, including the patients
that k-means gave away. The two small ellipses (normal and chemical) overlap,
and they keep overlapping at the end, because the two groups do overlap in the
data. A hard-assignment method cannot represent that overlap. A GMM can.

# Part 3 — Reading the fitted model

First, does the GMM recover the diagnoses?

```{webr}
gmm_cl <- apply(gmm3$r, 1, which.max)   # hard label: most probable cluster

table(diagnosis = dia$class, cluster = gmm_cl)
mean(gmm_cl == as.integer(dia$class))
```

Compare with k-means in Part 1. The share of patients in the "right" cluster
rises from 75% to 86%. 26 of the 36 chemical patients are in their own
cluster, up from 13. No overt patient is lost to the normal cluster any more.

```{webr}
dia |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(gmm_cl)) |>
  ggplot(aes(glucose, insulin)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = cluster, shape = class), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = ellipses_of(gmm3), aes(x, y, colour = cluster),
            linewidth = 1) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "GMM clusters (colour) vs. diagnosis (shape)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### The cluster descriptions

A GMM gives three deliverables (from the slides): labels, probabilities, and
**descriptions** of each cluster. The weights $\hat\pi_k$ say how common each
cluster is. The means $\hat\mu_k$ say where it sits. We map the means back to
clinical units:

```{webr}
mu_clinical <- sweep(sweep(gmm3$mu, 2, pp$std, "*"), 2, pp$mean, "+")
colnames(mu_clinical) <- colnames(z)

data.frame(cluster = 1:3,
           weight = round(gmm3$pi_k, 3),
           round(mu_clinical, 0))
```

The covariance matrices tell us how the tests move together **inside** each
cluster. The correlations:

```{webr}
for (k in 1:3) {
  cat("\nCluster", k, "- correlation matrix\n")
  print(round(cov2cor(gmm3$Sigma[[k]]), 2))
}
```

Inside a cluster, the tests are related, and the relations differ by cluster.
In the normal cluster, the tests are nearly unrelated (correlations 0.22 or
less). In the overt cluster, glucose and insulin responses move together
(correlation 0.95), and both fall as `sspg` rises (about -0.7). A model that
forces the correlations to zero, or the clusters to be round, misses this.
Part 6 tests that.

# Part 4 — Soft assignment: who is hard to place?

So far we used only the most probable cluster. The full output is the matrix of
responsibilities $r_{nk}$, one row per patient. The **highest** probability in
a row measures how sure the model is. Here are patient 1 and the three
patients the model is least sure about:

```{webr}
conf <- apply(gmm3$r, 1, max)

least_sure <- order(conf)[1:3]
round(gmm3$r[c(1, least_sure), ], 3)
dia$class[c(1, least_sure)]
```

Each row sums to 1. Patient 1 has a row like (0.99, 0.01, 0.00): clearly in
one cluster. The other three have probability split between two clusters:
they sit on a border.

Over all patients:

```{webr}
ggplot(data.frame(conf), aes(conf)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.9, colour = "#EE0000") +
  labs(x = "highest membership probability", y = "patients") +
  theme_bw()

sum(conf < 0.9)           # patients the model is less than 90% sure about
table(dia$class[conf < 0.9])
```

Most patients have a probability near 1. A group of 23 patients, left of the
red line, are uncertain. Which diagnosis do they have? 12 of the 23 are
**chemical** diabetes, the intermediate stage. That is one third of all
chemical patients. This is the clinical story: chemical diabetes sits
between normal and overt, and the model says so by splitting the probability
of those patients across clusters.

```{webr}
dia |>
  mutate(conf = conf) |>
  ggplot(aes(glucose, insulin, colour = conf)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "D", direction = -1, end = 0.9,
                         name = "highest\nprobability") +
  labs(title = "Dark points are the patients the model cannot place") +
  theme_bw()
```

k-means has no such output. It assigns every patient with full confidence,
including the ones that a clinician would call borderline. In practice, we can
use this: send patients below a probability threshold for a second look,
and treat the confident ones as settled.

**A warning.** The probabilities come from the model. They are only as good
as the assumption that each cluster is a normal distribution. A model with a
wrong shape gives confident but wrong probabilities.

# Part 5 — Choosing $K$

So far we used $K = 3$ because we know there are three diagnoses. In real
work we do not. The slides give two tools: BIC (parametric) and the silhouette
(non-parametric).

**BIC** rewards fit and penalizes parameters:
$$\text{BIC} = 2\,\ell(\hat\theta) - d \log N,$$
where $\ell$ is the log-likelihood and $d$ is the number of free parameters.
A full-covariance GMM with $K$ clusters in $p$ dimensions has
$d = K\left(p + \tfrac{p(p+1)}{2}\right) + (K - 1)$: a mean, a covariance, and
a weight per cluster (the weights sum to 1). **Higher BIC is better.**

```{webr}
bic <- function(f) {
  K <- length(f$pi_k)
  q <- switch(f$cov_type, full = p * (p + 1) / 2, diag = p, spherical = 1)
  d <- K * (p + q) + (K - 1)
  2 * tail(f$loglik, 1) - d * log(n)
}

Ks   <- 1:6
fits <- lapply(Ks, function(K) { set.seed(42); fit_gmm(z, K) })
bic_k <- sapply(fits, bic)

data.frame(K = Ks, loglik = round(sapply(fits, function(f) tail(f$loglik, 1)), 1),
           BIC = round(bic_k, 1))
```

The log-likelihood always rises with $K$. BIC peaks at $K = 3$ and then falls,
because extra clusters cost more in parameters than they gain in fit.

The silhouette needs hard labels. We use the GMM's most probable cluster, and
for comparison k-means labels:

```{webr}
library(cluster)
d <- dist(z)

sil_gmm <- sapply(2:6, function(K)
  mean(silhouette(apply(fits[[K]]$r, 1, which.max), d)[, "sil_width"]))
sil_km <- sapply(2:6, function(K) {
  set.seed(42)
  mean(silhouette(kmeans(z, K, nstart = 25)$cluster, d)[, "sil_width"])
})

p_bic <- ggplot(data.frame(K = Ks, BIC = bic_k), aes(K, BIC)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = Ks) +
  labs(title = "BIC (GMM): larger is better") + theme_bw()
p_sil <- ggplot(data.frame(K = rep(2:6, 2), sil = c(sil_gmm, sil_km),
                           labels = rep(c("GMM", "k-means"), each = 5)),
                aes(K, sil, colour = labels)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(y = "average silhouette width",
       title = "Silhouette: larger is better") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

grid.arrange(p_bic, p_sil, nrow = 1)
round(rbind(GMM = sil_gmm, kmeans = sil_km), 3)
```

BIC says $K = 3$. The silhouette says $K = 2$, for both methods, and gives
$K = 3$ a clearly lower value. Why?

The silhouette measures **compact, well-separated blobs**. The cleanest split
of these data is "overt" against "everyone else", because the overt group is
far away. The chemical and normal groups overlap, so splitting them lowers the
silhouette. BIC asks a different question: does a three-cluster *model* explain
the data better, given the cost of its parameters? Overlapping groups with
different shapes are exactly what a mixture model can represent.

Neither tool is always right. When they disagree, look at the clusters, and
ask someone who knows the domain. Here a clinician would not accept "overt
against everyone else", because chemical diabetes is a known, separate stage.

# Part 6 — Choosing the covariance shape

A GMM has a second choice that k-means does not have: the **shape** of each
cluster's covariance. The code from Part 2 supports three:

| `cov_type` | Each cluster is | Free covariance parameters per cluster |
|---|---|---|
| `"spherical"` | a round ball, with its own size | 1 |
| `"diag"` | an ellipse aligned with the axes (tests uncorrelated) | 3 |
| `"full"` | any ellipse, any tilt | 6 |

k-means is close to the first row, with all clusters the same size, and hard
assignments. We fit all three for $K = 1, \dots, 6$:

```{webr}
bic_by_shape <- bind_rows(lapply(c("spherical", "diag", "full"), function(ct) {
  b <- sapply(Ks, function(K) { set.seed(42); bic(fit_gmm(z, K, cov_type = ct)) })
  data.frame(K = Ks, BIC = b, shape = ct)
}))

ggplot(bic_by_shape, aes(K, BIC, colour = shape)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = Ks) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "BIC by number of clusters and covariance shape") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

bic_by_shape |> filter(K == 3) |> mutate(BIC = round(BIC, 1))
```

The full-covariance model has the best BIC by a wide margin, at $K = 3$ (-483,
against -559 for diagonal and -759 for spherical). Look at the other two
curves:

- **Diagonal** peaks later, around $K = 4$.
- **Spherical** is still rising at $K = 6$. A round ball is the wrong shape for
  a long thin cluster, so the model uses several balls to cover one band.

**The wrong covariance shape inflates the number of clusters.** This is the
GMM version of what happened to k-means in Part 1.

The three shapes also give different clusterings at $K = 3$:

```{webr}
agree <- sapply(c("spherical", "diag", "full"), function(ct) {
  set.seed(42)
  f <- fit_gmm(z, 3, cov_type = ct)
  mean(apply(f$r, 1, which.max) == as.integer(dia$class))
})
round(agree, 3)
```

Round clusters do about as badly as k-means (79% against 75%). Allowing
each cluster to stretch, with or without a tilt, gives 86%. The diagonal and
full models agree equally well with the diagnoses at $K = 3$. BIC still
prefers the full model. The three extra parameters per cluster (the
correlations) buy a much better fit, and the diagonal model needs a fourth
cluster to make up for the tilt it cannot represent.

# Part 7 — Starting points

EM climbs to a local maximum of the log-likelihood, so the start matters, just
as for k-means in Lab 7. We started from k-means, which is a good start. How
bad is a random one? We run EM 30 times from random cluster labels:

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
final_ll <- sapply(1:30, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  random_start <- sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE)
  tail(fit_gmm(z, K = 3, init = random_start)$loglik, 1)
})

ggplot(data.frame(ll = final_ll), aes(ll)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tail(gmm3$loglik, 1), colour = "#EE0000",
             linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "final log-likelihood", y = "runs (out of 30)",
       title = "EM from 30 random starts (red line: the k-means start)") +
  theme_bw()

mean(final_ll > tail(gmm3$loglik, 1) - 0.01)   # share of runs that reach the best fit
```

Only about **one run in five** reaches the best solution. The others stop at
worse local maxima, each with a different set of clusters, and nothing in the
output warns you. So:

- Start from several different initial clusterings, and keep the fit with the
  highest log-likelihood.
- Initializing from k-means is a common and good default.
- Set a seed so that you and your readers get the same clusters.

## Try it yourself

**1. A responsibility by hand.** For the least certain patient (`i`), compute $r_{nk}$ directly
from the formula, using `dmvnorm()`, and check that it equals that
patient's row of `gmm3$r`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_one_patient
i     <- least_sure[1]
x_i   <- z[i, ]
dens  <- sapply(1:3, function(k)
  gmm3$pi_k[k] * dmvnorm(x_i, gmm3$mu[k, ], gmm3$Sigma[[k]]))
r_i   <- dens / sum(______)
round(r_i, 3)
round(gmm3$r[i, ], 3)
```

**2. Four clusters.** Fit $K = 4$ with full covariances (`fits[[4]]`). Cross
the clusters with the diagnoses. Which diagnosis is split in two? Profile the
clusters in clinical units (copy the code from Part 3). Does the new cluster
make clinical sense?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_k4
f4 <- fit_gmm(z, K = ______)
table(diagnosis = dia$class, cluster = apply(f4$r, 1, which.max))
round(f4$pi_k, 3)
```

**3. A different threshold.** In Part 4, how many patients have a highest
probability below 0.7? Below 0.99? What is the diagnosis mix at each
threshold? What would be a sensible rule for sending patients for a second
look?

**4. Fewer tests.** A clinic may measure only glucose and insulin. Fit a GMM
to `z[, 1:2]` with $K = 3$ (the E-step and M-step work for any number of
columns, but `bic()` uses `p`, so skip BIC). How do the clusters compare with
the three-test fit?

## Things worth remembering

- **A GMM models the clusters; k-means only partitions the points.** Each
  cluster has a weight, a mean, and its own covariance matrix.
- **Soft assignment is the main gain.** The probability of belonging to each
  cluster shows who is borderline. Here the borderline patients were mostly
  the chemical, intermediate stage.
- **EM alternates two easy steps.** The E-step computes responsibilities.
  The M-step re-estimates parameters with those responsibilities as weights.
  The log-likelihood never goes down.
- **EM finds local maxima.** Use several starts and keep the best.
- **BIC and the silhouette answer different questions.** BIC asked whether a
  model fits well for its size. The silhouette asked whether the blobs are
  compact. They disagreed here, and a domain expert settles it.
- **The covariance shape is a modelling choice.** Too restrictive a shape
  (round, or axis-aligned) needs extra clusters to cover the data. Compare
  shapes by BIC.
- **The model is an assumption.** The probabilities are only as good as the
  normal-cluster assumption.
